metadata.basis: Official Module Content Review / Key Concept Review checklist mirrored in study-coverage.html and nur234.html .modunit .review-topics. Concise paraphrases of the linked course notes, ATI templates and instructor summaries; not quotations.
metadata.numberingNote: Use official review modules. Official M11 draws on legacy pages m11 and m13; M12 on m11; M13 on m12 and m14. Legacy page numbers are source locations, not the current exam module.
metadata.excludedSupportingLink: Methods and aftercare infographic is a resource within circumcision, not an additional review topic.
metadata.clinicalRules: Follow assigned Pillitteri/ATI exam conventions. Boggy uterus displaced right: empty bladder first, then massage. Boggy midline: massage first. Include oxygen by mask for PPH and cord prolapse. No lab-value question is introduced here.
metadata.visualPolicy: sn is an exact verified original handout title, or empty when no matching original was located. memory is a matching existing original mnemonic key; empty values use the new original mnemonic scene and caption. Do not substitute an unrelated picture.
knownCorrections: Review label Group B Streptococcus Aureus is corrected to Group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).
Misspelled Soft signs or labor is normalized to Early signs of labor.
metadata.sourceAccessNote: The complete website checklist and linked notes were used. Direct G-drive course-folder access was denied, so no claim is made that the original Drive review files were re-read.

topics.title: Reproductive life planning
topics.recognize: Pregnancy goals, medical history, STI exposure and ability to use a method guide reproductive planning.
topics.act: Ask privately about preferences, safety and access; support an informed, voluntary choice and teach correct use.
topics.remember: Pregnancy prevention and STI prevention are separate goals; condoms may accompany another contraceptive method.

topics.title: Fertility awareness
topics.recognize: Cervical mucus becomes clear/stretchy near ovulation; basal temperature rises after ovulation. Cycle tracking estimates fertile days.
topics.act: Teach consistent observations and abstinence or barrier use during the fertile window; assess whether cycles and routines support the method.
topics.remember: Basal temperature confirms ovulation afterward; it does not predict the fertile window by itself.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents cycle tracking: basal temperature rises after ovulation rather than predicting it alone.
topics.sn_note: Related physiology handout: use the course notes for complete fertility-awareness instructions.

topics.title: Contraception methods (natural / barrier / hormonal / surgical )
topics.recognize: Natural, barrier, hormonal and permanent methods differ in effectiveness, timing, contraindications and reversibility.
topics.act: Review health history, adherence, backup requirements and emergency contraception; teach condoms for STI-risk reduction.
topics.remember: IUDs/implants provide lasting reversible prevention; sterilization is intended to be permanent. Estrogen-containing methods require assessment of clot risk and other contraindications.

topics.title: Fetal growth and development / stages of development
topics.recognize: Embryonic organ formation occurs mainly during weeks 3–8 after fertilization; fetal growth and maturation follow.
topics.act: Clarify which pregnancy clock is being used when reviewing exposures, developmental milestones and screening dates.
topics.remember: Gestational age starts at the last menstrual period, about two weeks before conception; forming an organ does not mean it is mature.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents the embryo becoming a fetus; gestational dating begins about two weeks before conception.

topics.title: Embryonic and fetal structures
topics.recognize: The amnion surrounds the fluid cavity, the chorion contributes to the placental side, and the yolk sac supports early nutrition and blood-cell formation.
topics.act: Connect each structure with its job when reviewing fetal development and ultrasound findings.
topics.remember: Placenta, cord, membranes and fluid are supporting structures with different functions; they are not interchangeable names.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents fetal development supported by distinct membranes, placenta and early yolk-sac functions.

topics.title: Placental function
topics.recognize: The placenta exchanges oxygen, nutrients and wastes and produces hCG, progesterone, estrogen and hPL. Maternal and fetal blood normally remain separate.
topics.act: Review medication and substance exposures; teach avoiding alcohol and other harmful exposures.
topics.remember: The placenta transfers oxygen rather than manufacturing it, and it does not block every drug, toxin or infection.

topics.title: Amniotic membranes / fluid volumes
topics.recognize: Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus, supports movement and stabilizes temperature. Amnion and chorion form the membranes.
topics.act: Assess reported fluid leakage and follow ordered evaluation of membranes, fluid volume and fetal wellbeing.
topics.remember: Reduced fluid raises cord-compression concerns; excessive fluid can overdistend the uterus. A fluid abnormality requires evaluation of its cause.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents amniotic fluid cushioning the fetus; abnormal volume or leakage requires assessment.
topics.sn_note: Membrane-rupture handout; the course explanation also covers normal amniotic-fluid functions.

topics.title: Umbilical cord
topics.recognize: A normal cord has two arteries and one vein surrounded by protective Wharton's jelly.
topics.act: Identify vessel number and trace flow toward or away from the fetus; report an abnormal vessel count for further assessment.
topics.remember: The vein brings oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus; the arteries return blood toward the placenta.

topics.title: Origin and development of organ systems
topics.recognize: Ectoderm forms skin/nervous tissue; mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood and much cardiovascular/urinary tissue; endoderm forms much digestive/respiratory lining.
topics.act: Link exposure timing to developing organ systems and reinforce early prenatal care and prescribed folate.
topics.remember: Structural vulnerability is greatest during organ formation; growth and functional maturation continue later in pregnancy.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents three germ layers building different organ systems during embryonic development.

topics.title: AFP / chorionic villi / amniocentesis
topics.recognize: AFP is screening; CVS samples placental tissue and amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid for diagnostic testing.
topics.act: Explain purpose, risks and follow-up; support informed choice and ordered assessments before and after invasive testing.
topics.remember: Typical windows: CVS 10–13 weeks; AFP and amniocentesis commonly 15–20 weeks. An abnormal screen is not a confirmed diagnosis.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents screening versus diagnosis: an abnormal AFP result needs further evaluation.

topics.title: Evaluating fetal wellbeing
topics.recognize: Fetal movement, NST, biophysical profile and contraction stress testing assess wellbeing. A reactive NST and negative CST are reassuring.
topics.act: Report decreased movement promptly; arrange prescribed follow-up for nonreactive or concerning results.
topics.remember: At 32 weeks or later, reactive NST means two accelerations of at least 15 beats/min for 15 seconds in 20 minutes.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents timed fetal testing; reactive NST and negative CST are reassuring patterns.

topics.title: EDC/Nagel’s rule
topics.recognize: Naegele's rule estimates the due date from the first day of the last menstrual period.
topics.act: Subtract three months, add seven days and adjust the year; compare the estimate with menstrual history and ultrasound dating.
topics.remember: The rule assumes a regular 28-day cycle. It estimates a date rather than guaranteeing the day of birth.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents Naegele's date calculation: subtract three months, add seven days, adjust the year.

topics.title: Psychological changes of pregnancy
topics.recognize: Ambivalence, shifting attention and changing body image can occur as pregnancy becomes real. Readiness, culture, relationships and support shape adjustment.
topics.act: Invite concerns without judgment and assess coping, anxiety, depression, relationship safety and practical support.
topics.remember: Trimester tasks are a teaching framework: accept pregnancy, accept the fetus, then prepare for birth; people do not follow identical emotional stages.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents psychological adjustment to pregnancy, the fetus and preparing for birth at an individual pace.

topics.title: Physiological changes of pregnancy (trimester tasks)
topics.recognize: Blood volume and cardiac workload rise; renal filtration increases, and progesterone contributes to reflux and constipation. The growing uterus changes posture and venous return.
topics.act: Teach comfort measures and left-side positioning for supine hypotension; assess unexpected or severe symptoms.
topics.remember: Plasma expands more than red-cell mass, causing dilutional anemia; this is different from proven iron deficiency.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents expanding plasma volume that can dilute red cells during normal pregnancy adaptation.

topics.title: Emotional responses
topics.recognize: Mood shifts and mixed feelings may reflect changing roles, body image and expectations. Support and prior mental-health history influence the response.
topics.act: Ask what the pregnancy means to the person and family; assess persistent distress, impaired functioning and safety concerns.
topics.remember: Early ambivalence alone does not prove rejection, but persistent depression or anxiety should not be dismissed as normal pregnancy.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents listening to mixed emotions while assessing persistent distress and functioning.

topics.title: Couvade syndrome
topics.recognize: Some partners develop pregnancy-like physical or emotional symptoms, described as couvade syndrome. Their experience may accompany adjustment to the pregnancy and parenting role.
topics.act: Include the partner in discussion and teaching while assessing individual concerns and support needs.
topics.remember: Couvade describes a partner's response; it does not establish pregnancy or justify ignoring persistent symptoms needing evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents a partner's pregnancy-like response, called couvade, without establishing pregnancy.

topics.title: Signs of pregnancy (presumptive, probable, positive)
topics.recognize: Presumptive signs are subjective symptoms; probable signs include positive hCG testing and cervical changes; positive signs come directly from the fetus.
topics.act: Confirm pregnancy through appropriate clinical evaluation rather than symptoms alone.
topics.remember: Amenorrhea/quickening are presumptive; a positive pregnancy test is probable; fetal heart activity, ultrasound visualization or examiner-felt movement are positive.

topics.title: Prenatal care/screening
topics.recognize: Prenatal visits combine history, maternal/fetal assessment, screening and education to identify problems early. Needs vary with gestation and risk.
topics.act: Review medicines, psychosocial needs and warning signs; encourage scheduled visits and arrange barriers-to-care support.
topics.remember: Routine textbook visits become more frequent as birth approaches; high-risk findings require an individualized plan rather than waiting for the next routine visit.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents scheduled prenatal assessments that become more frequent as birth approaches.

topics.title: Terms related to pregnancy status
topics.recognize: Gravida counts pregnancies; para counts pregnancies reaching the course's gestational threshold, regardless of the number of infants or survival.
topics.act: Obtain the complete pregnancy history, including current pregnancy, losses, gestational ages and living children.
topics.remember: Twins count as one pregnancy and one qualifying birth event; they may count as two living children.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents one pregnancy containing twins: one pregnancy event, potentially two living children.

topics.title: Gestational classification/history / GTPAL
topics.recognize: GTPAL separates total pregnancies, term births, preterm births, losses and living children.
topics.act: Count each pregnancy outcome by gestational age, then count living children separately; include the current pregnancy in gravida.
topics.remember: Course thresholds: term at least 37 weeks; preterm 20–36 weeks 6 days; losses before 20 weeks. Multiples do not multiply the pregnancy count.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents counting pregnancy outcomes separately from the number of living children in GTPAL.

topics.title: Fundal height and fetal heart tones
topics.recognize: Fundal height follows gestational landmarks; Doppler fetal heart tones are generally heard around 10–12 weeks.
topics.act: Compare serial fundal measurements and fetal heart findings with dating and the clinical picture; investigate discrepancies rather than diagnosing from one measurement.
topics.remember: Fundus is near the pubic symphysis at 12 weeks and umbilicus at 20 weeks; ultrasound establishes dating more accurately.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents rising fundal landmarks compared with gestational dating and fetal heart findings.

topics.title: Pelvic anatomy / pelvic exam
topics.recognize: The pelvic inlet, midpelvis and outlet form the passage; ischial spines mark fetal station. Pelvic examination may include external, speculum and bimanual assessment.
topics.act: Explain the examination, obtain consent, preserve privacy and stop if consent is withdrawn.
topics.remember: Pelvic shape labels alone do not determine birth outcome; station is measured relative to the ischial spines.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents the pelvic passage; the ischial spines define zero station.

topics.title: Laboratory screenings
topics.recognize: Initial screening commonly includes CBC, blood type/Rh, antibody screen, urine culture and selected infection/immunity tests. Later tests address diabetes and GBS.
topics.act: Verify timing, review results, arrange indicated follow-up and explain the purpose of each screen.
topics.remember: A screening result identifies risk or need for evaluation; it does not replace diagnostic confirmation or clinical assessment.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents prenatal tests collected at appropriate gestational windows, with follow-up for abnormal findings.

topics.title: Danger signs during pregnancy
topics.recognize: Bleeding, fluid leakage, reduced fetal movement, severe headache, visual change, chest pain or breathing difficulty need assessment.
topics.act: Obtain relevant maternal/fetal findings and contact the obstetric team urgently; do not dismiss new severe symptoms as ordinary discomfort.
topics.remember: Mild expected adaptations differ from abrupt, persistent or severe changes. Visual symptoms with headache raise concern for hypertensive complications.

topics.title: Health promotion during pregnancy/self-care needs
topics.recognize: Pregnancy changes sleep, hygiene, activity, sexual comfort and medication needs; access and daily routines affect self-care.
topics.act: Ask about actual habits, provide practical comfort teaching, review all medicines/supplements and reinforce prenatal follow-up.
topics.remember: Avoid alcohol, smoking and unapproved drugs; health teaching should fit the person's circumstances and distinguish expected discomforts from symptoms needing evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents reviewing daily habits, medicines and exposures to support pregnancy self-care.

topics.title: Minor systemic body changes of pregnancy
topics.recognize: Reflux, constipation, urinary frequency, back discomfort and dependent leg swelling commonly accompany pregnancy adaptations.
topics.act: Offer small meals, appropriate fluids/fiber, body mechanics and position changes; assess severity and associated symptoms before reassuring.
topics.remember: Dyspnea at rest, dysuria/fever, sudden swelling with headache or persistent severe pain requires evaluation rather than routine comfort advice alone.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents discomforts that become sudden, severe or associated with warning signs.

topics.title: Effects of teratogens on fetus
topics.recognize: Teratogens can interfere with fetal development; alcohol, some medicines, infections and other exposures can cross the placenta.
topics.act: Review exposures and timing; reinforce prescribed folic acid and provider review of medicines before conception and throughout pregnancy.
topics.remember: Organ formation is particularly vulnerable to structural injury, while later exposures may affect growth or function; the placenta is not a complete barrier.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents developing organs that are vulnerable to harmful exposures during formation.

topics.title: Soft (early) signs of labor
topics.recognize: Lightening lowers the presenting part, easing breathing while increasing pelvic pressure; mucus plug passage may appear pink or blood-streaked.
topics.act: Explain what to monitor and when to contact the birth team, especially fluid leakage, heavy bleeding, reduced movement or symptoms before term.
topics.remember: These signs can precede labor; progressive cervical change with contractions establishes labor.

topics.title: Fluid needs during pregnancy
topics.recognize: Adequate fluids support circulation, bowel function and nutrition; vomiting or poor access can reduce intake.
topics.act: Encourage the course's usual goal of about 8–10 glasses of water daily unless the individual care plan limits fluids; assess dehydration and persistent vomiting.
topics.remember: Space fluids between meals when nausea interferes with eating; fluid advice must account for cardiac or renal restrictions.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents adequate hydration adapted to nausea and any prescribed fluid restrictions.

topics.title: Weight gain during pregnancy
topics.recognize: Recommended pregnancy gain depends on prepregnancy BMI and fetal number; the pattern matters alongside the total.
topics.act: Track weight over time and assess intake, food access and sudden changes; refer for individualized nutrition support when needed.
topics.remember: Singleton targets: underweight 28–40 lb, normal BMI 25–35, overweight 15–25, obesity 11–20. Sudden gain with concerning symptoms is not simply overeating.
topics.mnemonic: The balance represents weight-gain targets matched to prepregnancy BMI rather than one target for everyone.

topics.title: Nutrition needs during pregnancy (foods to limit/avoid)
topics.recognize: Pregnancy increases needs for iron, folate and other nutrients; food safety reduces infection risk.
topics.act: Teach balanced intake, prenatal supplements and safe preparation; avoid unpasteurized foods and raw/undercooked animal products, and heat deli meats until steaming.
topics.remember: Iron absorbs better with vitamin C than with milk or antacids. No extra first-trimester calories are routinely needed for a normal-BMI singleton pregnancy.

topics.title: Common problems affecting nutritional health during pregnancy (n/v, pica, pyrosis)
topics.recognize: Nausea/vomiting can reduce intake; pica means craving nonfood substances; pyrosis means heartburn.
topics.act: Try small frequent meals and dry food before rising; assess pica/iron status and persistent vomiting, weight loss or dehydration.
topics.remember: Pica can accompany iron deficiency. Persistent severe vomiting needs assessment for hyperemesis rather than reassurance that all morning sickness is harmless.
topics.mnemonic: The food symbol represents intake disrupted by nausea, nonfood cravings or heartburn; persistent problems need assessment.

topics.title: Women with unique needs (age, special diets, multiple gestation, hyperemesis gravidarum)
topics.recognize: Adolescence, restricted diets, multiple gestation, food insecurity and severe vomiting can make nutritional needs harder to meet.
topics.act: Assess the actual diet and barriers, arrange dietitian/food-support services and monitor weight, hydration and indicated laboratory trends.
topics.remember: Hyperemesis may require prescribed IV fluids, electrolyte correction and antiemetics; vegetarian eating requires planning for protein, iron, B12 and other nutrients.
topics.mnemonic: The food symbol represents nutrition plans tailored to age, dietary restrictions, multiple pregnancy or severe vomiting.

topics.title: Four P’s of labor (passage, passenger, powers, psyche)
topics.recognize: Labor progress depends on passage, passenger, powers and psyche: pelvic route, fetal factors, contractions/pushing and emotional response.
topics.act: Assess all four when progress slows, including bladder, positioning, support and fetal status.
topics.remember: Do not treat every slow labor with stronger contractions; a malpositioned passenger or obstructed passage needs a different response. Some resources add maternal position as a fifth P.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents labor depending on passage, passenger, powers and psyche—not contraction strength alone.
topics.sn_note: This original uses five Ps; the supplied course checklist groups passage, passenger, powers and psyche as four.

topics.title: Passenger (fetal skull, attitude, lie, presentation, position, engagement, station)
topics.recognize: Attitude is flexion; lie compares fetal/maternal spines; presentation names the leading part; position describes its orientation. Skull molding helps adaptation.
topics.act: Assess presentation, engagement and descent through examination/Leopold maneuvers and confirm uncertain findings as ordered.
topics.remember: Engagement is passage of the widest presenting diameter through the inlet; station describes descent relative to ischial spines, with zero at the spines.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents how fetal attitude, lie, presentation and position affect descent through the pelvic passage.

topics.title: Leopold maneuvers
topics.recognize: Abdominal palpation identifies the fetal part in the fundus, the back, presenting part and degree of descent.
topics.act: Explain the maneuvers, have the client empty the bladder and palpate systematically; use the fetal back to help locate heart tones.
topics.remember: Leopold maneuvers estimate lie/presentation and guide assessment; ultrasound can clarify uncertain presentation before procedures.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents systematic palpation to identify fetal lie, presenting part, back and descent.

topics.title: Contractions (frequency, duration, intensity)
topics.recognize: Frequency measures the start of one contraction to the start of the next; duration measures start to finish. Intensity is contraction strength.
topics.act: Assess the pattern, strength and uterine relaxation along with fetal response; recognize excessive activity and inadequate recovery time.
topics.remember: External tocodynamometry shows timing, not precise contraction pressure. Rest between contractions supports uteroplacental perfusion.
topics.mnemonic: The water symbol represents contraction waves: frequency is start-to-start; duration is start-to-finish; intensity is strength.

topics.title: Cervical changes (dilation, effacement)
topics.recognize: Dilation opens the cervix toward 10 cm; effacement thins it toward 100%.
topics.act: Follow cervical change together with contractions, fetal station and maternal/fetal status; support coping and explain progress without promising a fixed pace.
topics.remember: Regular contractions alone do not confirm true labor. Progressive dilation and effacement distinguish labor from contractions without cervical change.

topics.title: Stages/phases of labor
topics.recognize: First stage ends at full dilation; second ends with birth; third ends with placental delivery; fourth is early recovery.
topics.act: Match assessment/support to the stage and watch fetal tolerance during labor, then fundal tone, bleeding and vital signs after birth.
topics.remember: First-stage latent/active/transition phases describe progression; the second stage begins at full dilation, not with the first painful contraction.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents four labor stages ending with full dilation, birth, placental delivery and early recovery.

topics.title: Rupture of membranes
topics.recognize: A gush or persistent trickle may indicate membrane rupture; fluid appearance and fetal response matter.
topics.act: Check fetal heart rate promptly, note time/color/odor/amount, assess for prolapse when indicated and monitor temperature/infection signs; minimize unnecessary vaginal examinations.
topics.remember: Sudden fetal bradycardia after rupture can mean cord compression or prolapse, especially with a high presenting part.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents ruptured membranes, followed promptly by fetal heart-rate assessment.

topics.title: Maternal response to labor
topics.recognize: Contractions and pushing transiently increase cardiovascular workload; breathing, pulse and blood pressure can rise during effort. Nausea may reflect slowed gastric emptying.
topics.act: Support rest, position changes, appropriate hydration, bladder emptying and coping; compare findings between contractions.
topics.remember: Persistent tachycardia, hypotension, fever, hypoxemia or severe unexpected pain requires evaluation rather than being labeled a normal labor response.
topics.mnemonic: The balance represents maternal recovery between contraction efforts; persistent abnormal findings require evaluation.

topics.title: Fetal response to labor
topics.recognize: Contractions temporarily reduce uteroplacental flow; the fetus normally recovers during relaxation when reserve is adequate.
topics.act: Interpret baseline, variability, accelerations, decelerations and recovery together with maternal status and contraction activity.
topics.remember: Excess contractions, maternal hypotension or placental disease reduce reserve. A tracing feature alone does not establish the cause; assess the complete pattern.

topics.title: Fetal danger signs of labor  (meconium staining)
topics.recognize: Meconium-stained fluid, persistent abnormal heart-rate patterns or poor recovery can signal fetal compromise and need evaluation.
topics.act: Assess fetal heart rate and maternal/contraction status, notify the team and prepare appropriate newborn support at birth.
topics.remember: Meconium raises concern but is not, by itself, proof of hypoxia; persistent bradycardia or late decelerations requires prompt action.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents fetal danger cues that require assessment, including abnormal tracing or meconium-stained fluid.

topics.title: Fetal heart rate monitoring
topics.recognize: Assess baseline, variability, accelerations and decelerations in context; the usual baseline is 110–160 beats/min.
topics.act: Position external transducers appropriately and compare the tracing with contractions and maternal vital signs; investigate concerning patterns promptly.
topics.remember: Moderate variability generally supports adequate current oxygenation. External monitoring differs from a scalp electrode or intrauterine pressure catheter, which require appropriate access and precautions.

topics.title: Periodic changes (accelerations, decelerations)
topics.recognize: Accelerations are generally reassuring. Early decelerations mirror contractions; variable decelerations vary abruptly; late decelerations follow the contraction peak.
topics.act: Relate timing to contractions and assess variability, recovery and maternal status before deciding the response.
topics.remember: Early usually means head compression; variable means cord compression; late suggests impaired uteroplacental perfusion. Persistent abnormal patterns need intervention.

topics.title: Management of periodic changes
topics.recognize: Recurrent variable/late decelerations, prolonged deceleration or reduced variability can indicate impaired oxygen delivery.
topics.act: Reposition laterally, stop oxytocin when running, assess maternal pressure/contractions, support ordered fluids and oxygen per the course response sequence, and notify the team.
topics.remember: Treat the cause: variables suggest cord compression; late patterns suggest placental perfusion problems. Persistent abnormalities can require expedited birth.

topics.title: Induction/augmentation of labor
topics.recognize: Induction begins labor; augmentation improves labor already underway. Oxytocin and cervical-ripening methods can produce excess uterine activity.
topics.act: Confirm indication/consent and fetal status, use the ordered method and monitor contractions plus fetal response; stop oxytocin for tachysystole or concerning fetal intolerance.
topics.remember: A favorable cervix improves induction success. Stronger contractions cannot overcome an obstructed passage or contraindication to vaginal birth.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents labor being started or strengthened, with monitoring to prevent excessive contractions.

topics.title: Pain and comfort management during labor (pharmacological)
topics.recognize: Labor pain changes from visceral abdominal/back pain toward sharper perineal pain; systemic opioids and regional methods have different effects.
topics.act: Assess preferences, pain relief, breathing, sedation and fetal response; monitor carefully after medication and provide assistance with mobility.
topics.remember: Systemic opioids near birth can depress newborn respirations. Relief must be balanced with maternal/fetal safety, and comfort measures can continue alongside medication.
topics.mnemonic: The airway symbol represents respiratory monitoring when medication relieves labor pain.

topics.title: Complementary and alternative therapies for pain management
topics.recognize: Breathing, relaxation, massage, counterpressure, movement, heat and hydrotherapy may improve coping and reduce pain perception.
topics.act: Ask what feels helpful, adapt positioning and involve the chosen support person; assess response and maintain safety.
topics.remember: Nonpharmacologic comfort can continue with medication or an epidural. The client's preference can change during labor without representing failure.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents comfort and coping supported by the client's chosen nonpharmacologic techniques.

topics.title: Types of anesthesia used during labor
topics.recognize: Epidural analgesia supports ongoing labor; spinal anesthesia acts rapidly for selected births; pudendal block targets perineal pain. General anesthesia affects consciousness and airway protection.
topics.act: Monitor blood pressure, respirations, fetal response and bladder after regional anesthesia; treat hypotension and assist mobility until sensation/motor function returns.
topics.remember: Epidural hypotension can reduce placental perfusion. A pudendal block does not relieve contraction pain.
topics.mnemonic: The airway symbol represents anesthesia safety, including breathing, pressure and fetal-response monitoring.

topics.title: Identifying a high-risk pregnancy
topics.recognize: Risk may predate pregnancy or emerge later: cardiac, renal/endocrine disease, chronic hypertension, prior complications, multifetal pregnancy and care barriers matter.
topics.act: Establish baseline maternal/fetal findings, reconcile medicines and coordinate indicated specialist care and follow-up.
topics.remember: Risk identification should produce an individualized surveillance plan and clear urgent warning signs, not a label without practical support.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents extra surveillance tailored to the pregnancy's specific risks.

topics.title: Cardiovascular disorders and pregnancy (left sided and right sided failure)
topics.recognize: Left-sided heart failure causes pulmonary congestion, dyspnea, orthopnea and crackles; right-sided failure causes systemic congestion, edema and neck-vein distention.
topics.act: Escalate breathlessness at rest, chest pain, syncope or hypoxemia; trend oxygenation, perfusion, fluid balance and fetal status.
topics.remember: Pregnancy increases cardiac workload, and postpartum fluid shifts can also trigger decompensation; both failure patterns may coexist.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents congestion: fluid can back up into the lungs or systemic circulation.

topics.title: Chronic hypertensive vascular disease
topics.recognize: Hypertension present before pregnancy or before 20 weeks suggests chronic hypertension; new organ findings can indicate superimposed preeclampsia.
topics.act: Compare pressure, renal findings and urine protein with baseline; reinforce prescribed treatment and urgently report severe headache, visual change, upper abdominal pain or dyspnea.
topics.remember: Chronic hypertension does not protect against preeclampsia. Medication selection must account for pregnancy; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are generally avoided.
topics.memory_note: Related warning-sign visual: watch for superimposed preeclampsia in chronic hypertension.

topics.title: Venous thromboembolic disease
topics.recognize: Unilateral painful swelling, warmth or redness suggests DVT; sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis or collapse suggests pulmonary embolism.
topics.act: Escalate promptly, anticipate imaging and ordered anticoagulation, and avoid massaging the leg.
topics.remember: Heparin-based therapy is commonly used in pregnancy. Anticoagulation affects bleeding precautions, birth planning and neuraxial anesthesia; Homan's sign is not a reliable diagnostic test.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents a clot that can obstruct a vein or travel to the lungs.

topics.title: Renal / Urinary disorders of pregnancy (UTI’s)
topics.recognize: Cystitis causes dysuria, urgency or suprapubic discomfort; fever/flank pain suggests pyelonephritis. Asymptomatic bacteriuria can be found by prenatal culture.
topics.act: Obtain ordered urine studies, monitor maternal/fetal status and administer prescribed antibiotics; escalate systemic symptoms.
topics.remember: Pyelonephritis can cause sepsis and preterm labor and usually requires initial inpatient care; lack of urinary symptoms does not exclude bacteriuria.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents fever with flank pain: urinary infection may have reached the kidneys.

topics.title: Endocrine disorders and pregnancy (Diabetes mellitus)
topics.recognize: Pregestational and gestational diabetes differ in onset. Early hyperglycemia increases anomaly risk; later hyperglycemia promotes excessive fetal growth and neonatal hypoglycemia.
topics.act: Teach glucose monitoring, individualized food/activity plans, prescribed medication and hypoglycemia response; arrange fetal and postpartum follow-up.
topics.remember: After birth, maternal insulin needs can fall rapidly. The infant's high insulin can persist after maternal glucose delivery stops.
topics.mnemonic: The balance represents changing glucose and insulin needs before and immediately after birth.

topics.title: Spontaneous abortions
topics.recognize: Bleeding/cramps may accompany miscarriage. Threatened loss has a closed cervix; incomplete loss retains tissue, while complete loss passes it.
topics.act: Assess stability and escalate heavy bleeding, syncope, fever or worsening pain; support ultrasound/hCG evaluation, treatment choices and grief care.
topics.remember: Symptoms alone do not establish viability or pregnancy location; routine bed rest does not prevent miscarriage.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents urgent evaluation of heavy bleeding, faintness or fever during suspected pregnancy loss.

topics.title: Ectopic pregnancy
topics.recognize: Ectopic implantation can cause unilateral pelvic pain and bleeding; rupture may cause shoulder pain, fainting and shock despite little visible blood.
topics.act: Assess circulation and urgently escalate suspected rupture; anticipate ultrasound/hCG evaluation and medical or surgical treatment according to stability.
topics.remember: An empty uterus alone does not diagnose ectopic pregnancy. Methotrexate treatment requires reliable follow-up and urgent reporting of worsening symptoms.

topics.title: Gestational trophoblastic disease
topics.recognize: Molar pregnancy may produce bleeding, marked nausea, high hCG and a uterus larger than expected; ultrasound/pathology establish the diagnosis.
topics.act: Support evacuation and serial hCG follow-up, contraception counseling and grief care.
topics.remember: Persistent trophoblastic disease can remain after evacuation. Follow-up duration depends on diagnosis and specialist protocol; a new pregnancy can obscure hCG monitoring.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents abnormal trophoblastic growth that still requires monitoring after evacuation.

topics.title: Premature cervical dilation
topics.recognize: Cervical insufficiency commonly causes painless shortening/dilation in the second trimester; prior midtrimester loss or preterm birth increases concern.
topics.act: Review cervical-length findings and history; support prescribed progesterone/cerclage care and teach reporting pressure, bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or contractions.
topics.remember: Painless cervical opening differs from preterm labor driven by contractions with cervical change; not every short cervix receives the same treatment.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents a cervix opening too early, sometimes without painful contractions.

topics.title: Placenta previa
topics.recognize: Placenta over the cervical opening classically causes painless bleeding, but ultrasound determines location.
topics.act: Assess maternal circulation and fetal status; obtain urgent obstetric evaluation and prepare the ordered birth/bleeding plan.
topics.remember: Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until previa is excluded. Painless bleeding suggests previa but does not confirm it or measure hemorrhage severity.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents the cervical opening covered by placenta: avoid a digital examination until previa is excluded.

topics.title: Placental abruption
topics.recognize: Placental separation can cause abdominal/back pain, uterine tenderness or rigidity and fetal compromise; blood may remain concealed.
topics.act: Escalate urgently, quantify visible loss, assess perfusion/fetal status and prepare IV access, blood studies/products and possible urgent birth.
topics.remember: Small visible blood loss does not exclude major hemorrhage. Watch for DIC; abruption is separation, unlike previa's abnormal location.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents hemorrhage that may remain hidden behind a separated placenta.

topics.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
topics.recognize: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing widespread clotting and bleeding; oozing, bruising and worsening perfusion are warning signs.
topics.act: Treat the precipitating emergency with the team, support oxygenation/circulation and anticipate blood products plus serial coagulation studies.
topics.remember: Abruption, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, sepsis, major hemorrhage and amniotic fluid embolism are important obstetric triggers; trends matter more than one laboratory result.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents clotting supplies being consumed, followed by uncontrolled bleeding.

topics.title: Preterm labor
topics.recognize: Preterm labor occurs before 37 weeks with contractions and cervical change; pressure, cramps, backache or leaking fluid warrant evaluation.
topics.act: Assess membranes, infection, bleeding and fetal status; prepare prescribed corticosteroids, short-term tocolysis or transfer when appropriate.
topics.remember: Steroids promote fetal maturation; tocolytics buy time; magnesium may provide early-gestation neuroprotection. Infection or maternal/fetal compromise can make delaying birth unsafe.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents buying limited time for fetal maturation or transfer, not stopping labor at any cost.

topics.title: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
topics.recognize: Preeclampsia is hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or qualifying organ dysfunction; severe headache, visual changes or epigastric pain are concerning.
topics.act: Escalate severe findings. During magnesium, assess respirations, reflexes and urine output; stop suspected toxic infusion, support breathing and prepare ordered calcium gluconate.
topics.remember: Magnesium prevents/treats seizures; a separate antihypertensive treats severe pressure. Proteinuria is not required with qualifying organ dysfunction.

topics.title: HELLP syndrome
topics.recognize: HELLP means hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. RUQ/epigastric pain, nausea, malaise or headache can accompany it.
topics.act: Escalate suspected HELLP, assess bleeding/perfusion and anticipate serial blood counts, liver/renal tests, coagulation studies and an obstetric delivery plan.
topics.remember: Severe hypertension or proteinuria may be absent; concerning pain and laboratory trends still require action, including postpartum surveillance.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents RUQ pain with hemolysis, liver injury and low platelets—even without striking hypertension.

topics.title: Multiple gestation
topics.recognize: Multiple gestation increases preterm birth, growth, anemia, hypertension and uterine-overdistention risks; shared placentas add specific complications.
topics.act: Review ultrasound findings about fetal number and shared placenta/sacs; individualize nutrition, growth/fluid surveillance and maternal/newborn birth resources.
topics.remember: Chorionicity and amnionicity matter beyond counting fetuses; a shared placenta can create twin-to-twin transfusion risk.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents more than one fetus sharing resources, requiring tailored growth and placental surveillance.

topics.title: Amniotic fluid volume
topics.recognize: Oligohydramnios can accompany rupture, placental insufficiency or fetal urinary problems; polyhydramnios can accompany diabetes or impaired fetal swallowing.
topics.act: Assess membranes, growth and fetal wellbeing; interpret ultrasound volume with gestation and the suspected cause.
topics.remember: Low fluid increases cord-compression concerns; high fluid increases overdistention, preterm-labor and postpartum-atony risk. Volume alone does not identify the cause.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents too little or too much amniotic fluid, each creating different fetal and labor risks.

topics.title: Isoimmunization/Rhogam
topics.recognize: An Rh-negative person may form antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive fetal blood; those antibodies can affect a future/current Rh-positive fetus.
topics.act: Verify blood type and antibody screen; administer ordered Rh immune globulin to eligible unsensitized patients around 28 weeks and within 72 hours after an Rh-positive birth.
topics.remember: Prophylaxis prevents sensitization; it does not reverse established antibodies.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents Rh immune globulin preventing sensitization before antibodies form.

topics.title: Dysfunctional labor
topics.recognize: Slow labor can reflect ineffective powers, fetal malposition, a restricted passage or poor coping/support.
topics.act: Assess contraction pattern, cervical change, descent, bladder and maternal/fetal status; address the cause and reassess response.
topics.remember: More oxytocin is not the answer to every slow labor. Obstruction or fetal intolerance requires obstetric reassessment rather than simply stronger contractions.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents slow progress: assess why passage is blocked before increasing the pushing force.

topics.title: Group B streptococcus (GBS)
topics.recognize: GBS colonization can expose the newborn during birth; late-pregnancy screening generally occurs at 36–37 weeks.
topics.act: Verify results/allergies and administer indicated IV intrapartum antibiotics; communicate treatment timing and relevant history to the newborn team.
topics.remember: GBS is Streptococcus agalactiae, not Staphylococcus aureus. Colonization is not an STI; a prior affected infant or GBS bacteriuria can also establish prophylaxis indications.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents intrapartum antibiotics reducing early newborn infection after GBS exposure.

topics.title: Induction / Augmentation of labor
topics.recognize: Induction starts labor; augmentation strengthens established labor. Oxytocin/ripening can cause tachysystole and fetal intolerance.
topics.act: Confirm readiness, presentation, consent and contraindications; monitor fetal/contraction response and reduce or stop oxytocin for excessive activity according to the response protocol.
topics.remember: Tachysystole is more than five contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes; the fetus needs recovery between contractions.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents contraction spacing: too many contractions leave too little recovery time.

topics.title: Cervical ripening/Bishop score
topics.recognize: Bishop scoring combines cervical dilation, effacement, consistency, position and fetal station. A higher score indicates a more favorable cervix.
topics.act: Explain the sequence and prepare prescribed balloon or medication ripening when indicated; assess uterine-scar precautions and monitor contractions/fetal response.
topics.remember: Bishop predicts induction readiness, not spontaneous labor onset. An unfavorable cervix may need ripening before oxytocin.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents cervical readiness: a favorable Bishop score describes a doorway more prepared for induction.

topics.title: Uterine rupture/uterine inversion
topics.recognize: Rupture can cause fetal bradycardia, pain, bleeding, loss of station or shock. Inversion turns the uterus inside out after birth, causing hemorrhage/shock.
topics.act: Activate emergency help and resuscitation; stop oxytocin for suspected rupture and prepare surgery. For inversion, prepare trained-clinician replacement.
topics.remember: Do not pull the cord or independently remove placenta during inversion; both conditions demand immediate obstetric care.
topics.mnemonic: The uterus represents two distinct emergencies: a torn wall is rupture; turning inside out is inversion.

topics.title: Amniotic fluid embolism
topics.recognize: Amniotic fluid embolism can cause sudden respiratory/cardiovascular collapse during labor or shortly after birth, often followed by DIC.
topics.act: Activate obstetric/resuscitation teams, support oxygenation and ventilation, begin CPR if pulseless and coordinate hemorrhage management and urgent birth when indicated.
topics.remember: AFE is a clinical emergency without a single confirmatory test; team interventions occur simultaneously.
topics.mnemonic: The airway symbol represents sudden respiratory collapse requiring immediate resuscitation alongside circulatory support.

topics.title: Umbilical cord prolapse
topics.recognize: Cord prolapse may follow membrane rupture with a high presenting part; sudden fetal bradycardia/prolonged deceleration suggests compression.
topics.act: Call help, stop oxytocin, elevate the presenting part as trained, position to relieve compression, provide oxygen by mask and prepare urgent birth.
topics.remember: Maintain pressure relief until handover/birth; avoid unnecessary cord handling and never push the cord back into the uterus.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents the presenting part compressing the cord; lift pressure away and maintain relief until birth.

topics.title: Posterior/breech position
topics.recognize: Occiput posterior can produce back pain, slow rotation and prolonged labor; breech presents buttocks or feet first.
topics.act: Support position changes for posterior position; confirm breech and coordinate the individualized birth plan and monitoring.
topics.remember: Persistent malpresentation raises risks such as cord prolapse and may require cesarean birth; stronger contractions do not correct every position problem.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents a passenger facing the wrong direction or entering feet first, changing the birth plan.

topics.title: Macrosomia
topics.recognize: Large fetal size increases shoulder dystocia, maternal trauma and neonatal metabolic risks, but estimated weight is imprecise.
topics.act: Review growth/diabetes history, prepare for the planned birth and assess the newborn for injury and indicated glucose monitoring.
topics.remember: A large infant does not inevitably develop dystocia, and smaller infants can also have it; the whole labor assessment matters.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents increased fetal size, prompting preparation for difficult birth and newborn glucose problems.

topics.title: Shoulder dystocia
topics.recognize: After the head delivers, an impacted shoulder prevents the body from following; head retraction may create the turtle sign.
topics.act: Call the emergency team, record times and assist McRoberts positioning with directed suprapubic pressure; assess maternal/newborn injury after birth.
topics.remember: Never apply fundal pressure or excessive traction on the head; those actions can worsen impaction and injury.

topics.title: Inlet/outlet contraction
topics.recognize: A restricted inlet can prevent engagement; a restricted outlet can obstruct descent or delivery. Size and fetal position influence the fit.
topics.act: Monitor descent, cervical progress, contractions and fetal condition; escalate persistent obstruction for obstetric reassessment and possible cesarean birth.
topics.remember: Do not use oxytocin to force a fetus through an obstructed passage. A pelvic label alone does not determine outcome.
topics.mnemonic: The gate represents a narrowed inlet or outlet: extra force cannot safely solve an obstructed passage.

topics.title: External cephalic version
topics.recognize: ECV is external abdominal manipulation by a trained clinician to turn breech toward a head-down presentation.
topics.act: Confirm eligibility/consent, ultrasound findings and fetal wellbeing; monitor before/after in a setting able to perform urgent cesarean birth, and assess indicated Rh prophylaxis.
topics.remember: Report bleeding, pain, contractions, reduced movement or leaking fluid afterward; ECV can cause fetal intolerance.
topics.mnemonic: The newborn symbol represents turning the fetal presentation, with fetal assessment before and after the attempt.

topics.title: Forceps/Vacuum-assisted delivery
topics.recognize: Forceps or vacuum may expedite selected second-stage births when prerequisites are met.
topics.act: Verify full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, empty bladder, consent and analgesia; monitor fetal status and assess maternal/newborn trauma afterward.
topics.remember: Operative vaginal birth requires a trained operator and backup plan. Scalp swelling, neurologic change or excessive bleeding needs evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents prerequisites and injury checks that protect parent and infant during assisted vaginal birth.

topics.title: Velamentous insertion
topics.recognize: With velamentous insertion, fetal vessels travel through membranes without normal Wharton's-jelly protection before entering the placenta.
topics.act: Communicate ultrasound findings and follow the individualized surveillance/birth plan; assess whether vessels also cross near the cervix.
topics.remember: Unprotected vessels are vulnerable to compression or rupture. Velamentous insertion and vasa previa are related, but they are not identical conditions.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents exposed fetal vessels lacking their normal protective jelly.

topics.title: Vasa-previa
topics.recognize: Vasa previa places unprotected fetal vessels over or near the cervical opening; rupture may cause rapid fetal blood loss.
topics.act: Escalate bleeding with sudden fetal compromise after membrane rupture; avoid amniotomy when vasa previa is known/suspected and follow the specialist birth plan.
topics.remember: The blood loss is fetal, so maternal vital signs may initially appear stable.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents fetal blood at risk when unprotected vessels cross the cervical opening.

topics.title: Placenta accreta/increta/percreta
topics.recognize: Accreta attaches abnormally to myometrium; increta invades it; percreta extends through the uterine wall and possibly nearby organs.
topics.act: Prepare coordinated obstetric/surgical care with blood-product availability; explain the individualized plan, which may include hysterectomy.
topics.remember: Attempted placental separation can cause massive hemorrhage. Do not forcibly remove the placenta; prior cesarean plus previa raises concern.
topics.mnemonic: The uterus represents increasing depth of placental attachment, invasion and penetration through its wall.

topics.title: Amniotomy
topics.recognize: Amniotomy intentionally ruptures membranes to assist selected labor or monitoring procedures; cord compression/prolapse and infection are risks.
topics.act: Verify indication, presentation and engagement; assess fetal heart rate before and immediately afterward, and document fluid/time.
topics.remember: Continue infection surveillance and minimize unnecessary vaginal examinations after rupture; placental or fetal-vessel contraindications must be excluded first.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents artificial membrane rupture, followed immediately by checking the fetal heart rate.

topics.title: Episiotomy
topics.recognize: Episiotomy incises the perineum for selected birth circumstances. After repair, assess pain, swelling, wound approximation and bleeding.
topics.act: Provide ordered analgesia and perineal care; teach hygiene and reporting worsening pain, pressure, discharge or fever.
topics.remember: Severe persistent pain or pressure may indicate a hematoma rather than expected soreness; routine episiotomy is not required for every vaginal birth.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents severe pressure or escalating perineal pain after repair, which may signal a concealed hematoma.

topics.title: Internal monitoring
topics.recognize: A fetal scalp electrode measures fetal heart rate; an intrauterine pressure catheter measures contraction pressure and resting tone.
topics.act: Confirm ruptured membranes, appropriate access and contraindication review; maintain asepsis and assess for infection/trauma.
topics.remember: The devices answer different questions and do not replace maternal/fetal assessment; relevant infection or bleeding risks can make internal monitoring unsuitable.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents direct monitoring: one device watches fetal heart rate, another measures uterine pressure.

topics.title: Cesarean birth
topics.recognize: Cesarean birth requires surgical, anesthesia and newborn preparation, followed by monitoring for hemorrhage, infection, respiratory effects and VTE.
topics.act: Verify consent/allergies and ordered IV, antibiotics and thrombosis measures; afterward assess vitals, fundus/lochia, incision, urine, pain and mobility.
topics.remember: Encourage appropriate early movement and feeding support. Heavy bleeding, chest pain, dyspnea, fever or a swollen painful leg needs urgent evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents surgical preparation followed by postpartum surveillance for bleeding, infection and clots.

topics.title: Puerperium retrogressive and progressive changes
topics.recognize: Retrogressive changes reverse pregnancy adaptations, including uterine/vaginal involution; progressive changes include lactation, return of reproductive function and the parenting role.
topics.act: Assess physical recovery, feeding and adjustment together; support rest, comfort, education and follow-up.
topics.remember: Different systems recover at different rates. Postpartum care includes both returning toward baseline and developing new functions, not merely watching bleeding.
topics.mnemonic: The balance represents recovery of pregnancy changes alongside new lactation and parenting functions.

topics.title: Attachment/bonding
topics.recognize: Attachment develops through interaction; pain, fatigue, depression, difficult birth or separation can interfere.
topics.act: Offer skin-to-skin, rooming-in, feeding/care participation and practical support; include partners and assess persistent withdrawal or distress.
topics.remember: Bonding may take time. Do not assume poor attachment from one interaction, but investigate sustained lack of interest and barriers to safe infant care.
topics.mnemonic: The newborn symbol represents repeated supportive interaction that builds attachment over time.

topics.title: Disillusionment / postpartum blues
topics.recognize: Actual parenting or the baby's characteristics may differ from expectations; transient tearfulness and mood shifts can occur during early postpartum adjustment.
topics.act: Invite feelings without judgment, arrange rest/practical help and assess mood, functioning and safety.
topics.remember: Baby blues should resolve within about two weeks; persistent, worsening or disabling symptoms need assessment rather than reassurance alone.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents changing postpartum emotions; persistent impairment needs assessment beyond reassurance about baby blues.

topics.title: Uterine involution
topics.recognize: A normally involuting fundus is firm, midline and descends over time; a boggy or high/right-displaced fundus is concerning.
topics.act: For a boggy right-displaced uterus, empty the bladder first, then reassess/massage; for a boggy midline uterus, massage first.
topics.remember: Assess bleeding and perfusion and summon help for hemorrhage; a full bladder can prevent effective contraction.
topics.memory_note: Related postpartum-bleeding visual; use the fundal assessment sequence in the explanation.

topics.title: Lochia
topics.recognize: Lochia progresses rubra to serosa to alba and should generally lighten; heavier bleeding, large clots or foul odor requires assessment.
topics.act: Check color, amount and associated fundal/vital-sign findings; quantify concerning loss rather than relying on visual estimates alone.
topics.remember: Persistent or renewed heavy red bleeding is not ordinary progression. A firm fundus with continued bleeding raises concern for causes other than atony.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents lochia that should lighten, with heavier or persistent red flow requiring assessment.

topics.title: Cervical/vaginal involution
topics.recognize: The cervix narrows/firms after birth; vaginal swelling resolves as tissue heals. After vaginal birth the cervical opening commonly remains slit-shaped.
topics.act: Assess pain, wound approximation, discharge and function; teach perineal care and discuss lactation-related dryness.
topics.remember: Healing takes time, but worsening pain, concerning drainage or persistent functional problems need review rather than being labeled inevitable recovery.
topics.mnemonic: The uterus represents gradual postpartum tissue recovery, while persistent pain or abnormal discharge needs evaluation.

topics.title: Systemic changes during post-partum
topics.recognize: Postpartum fluid shifts alter cardiac workload; diuresis removes extra fluid, while retention can impair uterine contraction. Constipation and perineal discomfort are common.
topics.act: Assess perfusion, voiding, bowel function, mobility and healing; support fluids, comfort and activity as appropriate.
topics.remember: Dyspnea, chest pain, fever, severe headache or heavy bleeding is not routine recovery and requires urgent assessment.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents postpartum fluid shifts and the need to assess both circulation and bladder emptying.

topics.title: Preparation for discharge
topics.recognize: Discharge readiness includes physical recovery, safe self/infant care, support and a clear follow-up plan.
topics.act: Use teach-back for lochia/wound care, medications, feeding, activity, contraception and urgent symptoms; arrange indicated immunizations/Rh prophylaxis and support.
topics.remember: Ovulation can precede the first period. Heavy bleeding, chest pain, dyspnea, severe headache, fever or thoughts of harm require prompt help.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents a discharge plan that combines daily care, warning signs and follow-up.

topics.title: Lactation / colostrum
topics.recognize: Colostrum is present early and supplies protein and antibodies; milk volume rises over the following days. Prolactin supports production and oxytocin milk ejection.
topics.act: Support skin-to-skin, early feeding, effective latch and frequent feeding cues; assess painful latch rather than simply advising longer feeds.
topics.remember: Small early colostrum volume does not mean there is no milk; assess transfer and newborn intake.
topics.mnemonic: The food symbol represents antibody-rich colostrum feeding the newborn before larger milk volumes arrive.

topics.title: Assessing the newborn for adequate nutrition/nutritional allowances
topics.recognize: Adequate intake is reflected by observed milk transfer, age-appropriate wet/stool output and weight trend; poor feeding, lethargy or reduced urine needs assessment.
topics.act: Observe latch and swallowing, review output/weights and arrange feeding help when needed.
topics.remember: Aim for 8–12 breastfeeds daily; by about day five, at least six wet diapers is reassuring. Do not judge intake from feeding duration alone.

topics.title: Benefits of breastfeeding (maternal/fetal)
topics.recognize: Human milk provides nutrition and immune protection; breastfeeding also supports bonding and oxytocin-mediated uterine involution.
topics.act: Explain benefits, assess the family's informed feeding preference and provide practical latch/feeding support without judgment.
topics.remember: Colostrum's antibodies matter even before milk volume increases. Maternal benefits include lower breast/ovarian cancer risk; feeding safety and adequate infant intake remain priorities for every family.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents immune protection from human milk and supportive care for the family's feeding choice.

topics.title: Engorgement
topics.recognize: Engorgement causes fullness, swelling and discomfort, often when milk volume rises or feeding is ineffective/infrequent.
topics.act: Assess latch and transfer, support frequent effective feeds and use the course's comfort measures: warmth briefly before feeding and cold afterward/between feeds.
topics.remember: A focal red painful breast with fever or flu-like symptoms needs evaluation for mastitis rather than routine engorgement advice alone.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents milk accumulating when transfer is ineffective, making latch and feeding assessment important.
topics.sn_note: Related breastfeeding-technique handout; engorgement care is summarized in the explanation.

topics.title: Formula feeding
topics.recognize: Formula feeding requires correct dilution, hygienic preparation and responsive feeding; over-dilution reduces nutrition and can cause harm.
topics.act: Teach exact package preparation, safe storage and supported feeding; never prop bottles or microwave them, and discard leftovers one hour after feeding starts.
topics.remember: Follow newborn hunger/fullness cues and monitor output/weight. Do not stretch formula with extra water.
topics.mnemonic: The food symbol represents correctly prepared formula: changing the water-to-powder ratio changes safety and nutrition.

topics.title: Postpartum hemorrhage (tone/trauma/tissue/thrombin)
topics.recognize: PPH: cumulative loss of at least 1,000 mL after vaginal or cesarean birth, OR bleeding with hypovolemia within 24 hours. Four Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin.
topics.act: Call help; assess fundus/bladder, quantify loss, give oxygen by mask and support ordered IV fluids, uterotonics and blood.
topics.remember: Boggy/right-displaced: empty bladder first, then massage; boggy/midline: massage first. Firm but bleeding: consider trauma, retained tissue or coagulopathy. Do not wait for a volume threshold to act.
topics.sn_note: Original retains older blood-loss thresholds. Professor Buhler says to use 1,000 mL for either vaginal or cesarean birth; act on hypovolemia without waiting for that volume.

topics.title: Subinvolution
topics.recognize: Subinvolution is delayed return of the uterus toward its prepregnant state; persistent red lochia and an unexpectedly enlarged fundus raise concern.
topics.act: Assess bleeding, uterine findings, infection signs and vital trends; report abnormalities and prepare evaluation for retained tissue or infection.
topics.remember: This is delayed involution, not expected afterpains. Management targets the cause and ongoing hemorrhage risk.
topics.mnemonic: The uterus represents a fundus that is not shrinking as expected, especially with persistent red lochia.
topics.sn_note: Original retains older blood-loss thresholds. Professor Buhler says to use 1,000 mL for either vaginal or cesarean birth; act on hypovolemia without waiting for that volume.

topics.title: Puerperal infection
topics.recognize: Endometritis can cause fever, uterine tenderness, pelvic pain and foul/purulent lochia; wounds or urinary infection can also cause postpartum illness.
topics.act: Assess vitals, pain, fundus, lochia, incisions and breasts; obtain ordered cultures and start prescribed antibiotics promptly.
topics.remember: Prolonged membrane rupture, cesarean birth, repeated examinations and retained fragments raise risk. Worsening perfusion or mental status requires sepsis escalation.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents postpartum fever with uterine tenderness or foul lochia, prompting infection and sepsis assessment.
topics.sn_note: Endometritis is the uterine-infection example within the broader puerperal-infection topic.

topics.title: Mastitis
topics.recognize: Mastitis may cause a focal red, hot, painful breast with fever and flu-like symptoms; milk stasis and nipple trauma contribute.
topics.act: Assess feeding technique and symptoms, arrange treatment and prescribed antibiotics when indicated, and support ongoing breastfeeding or expression as tolerated.
topics.remember: Abruptly stopping milk removal can worsen stasis; persistent focal swelling or failure to improve needs further evaluation.
topics.mnemonic: The fire represents focal breast inflammation with systemic symptoms, distinct from uncomplicated fullness.

topics.title: Thrombophlebitis
topics.recognize: Unilateral leg warmth, pain, swelling or redness suggests thrombophlebitis; sudden chest pain/dyspnea suggests pulmonary embolism.
topics.act: Report findings, compare leg measurements, anticipate prescribed anticoagulation and use ordered elevation/warm compresses; never massage the affected limb.
topics.remember: Prevention includes appropriate early mobility; management of a suspected or confirmed clot follows the individualized treatment plan rather than unsupervised exercise.
topics.mnemonic: The blood symbol represents a venous clot: avoid massage and urgently report chest or breathing symptoms.

topics.title: GU system disorders
topics.recognize: Anesthesia, edema or trauma may cause retention/overflow leakage; dysuria, fever or flank pain raises infection concern.
topics.act: Assess bladder distention, ability to void and urine output; follow ordered bladder-emptying and infection evaluation/treatment plans.
topics.remember: A full bladder can impair uterine contraction and increase bleeding risk. Persistent incontinence, pain or difficulty voiding warrants follow-up rather than dismissal as normal childbirth recovery.
topics.mnemonic: The water container represents a bladder that must empty to support uterine contraction and recovery.

topics.title: Postpartum depression / psychosis
topics.recognize: Depression causes persistent sadness, anxiety or impaired functioning; psychosis may involve delusions, hallucinations, confusion or paranoia.
topics.act: Screen and ask directly about self/infant-harm thoughts; arrange treatment/support. For psychosis or immediate danger, protect parent/infant, stay with the client and obtain emergency help.
topics.remember: Baby blues are brief and self-limited; loss of reality or safety concerns is an emergency, not ordinary adjustment.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents postpartum mood assessment; hallucinations or delusions signal an emergency rather than ordinary blues.
topics.sn_note: This original covers blues and depression; the explanation also covers psychosis as an emergency.

topics.title: Infant with illness/physical challenge
topics.recognize: Infant illness or physical differences may bring fear, guilt, grief and loss of control, while separation can complicate bonding.
topics.act: Explain the condition plainly, check understanding and invite safe participation in comfort/care; coordinate NICU teaching, specialists, social work and peer support.
topics.remember: Family involvement should match the infant's condition and the family's readiness, without forcing a particular emotional response.
topics.mnemonic: The newborn symbol represents including the family safely in care despite illness or a physical difference.

topics.title: Neonatal death
topics.recognize: Neonatal death creates bereavement while the parent still needs postpartum physical recovery and follow-up. Families differ in cultural, spiritual and memory-making preferences.
topics.act: Offer privacy, honest compassionate explanations and choices about time with the infant; coordinate bereavement resources and continued care.
topics.remember: Do not impose a grief timetable or pressure the family to accept or decline contact and keepsakes.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents protecting the family's privacy, choices and ongoing postpartum care during bereavement.

topics.title: Vital sign measurement in the newborn
topics.recognize: Assess newborn heart rate, respirations, temperature, color and effort. Usual course ranges are heart rate 110–160/min, respirations 30–60/min and axillary temperature 36.5–37.5°C.
topics.act: Count carefully, trend findings and evaluate abnormal breathing, temperature instability or poor perfusion promptly.
topics.remember: Irregular breathing can occur, but grunting, flaring, retractions or central cyanosis is not a routine normal finding.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents careful newborn vital-sign counting and trending, especially irregular respirations.

topics.title: Systemic physiologic adaptation (cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, neuromuscular)
topics.recognize: Lung expansion begins air breathing and lowers pulmonary resistance; loss of placental circulation raises systemic resistance and changes fetal shunt flow.
topics.act: Assess respiratory effort, oxygenation/perfusion, feeding, stool passage, flexed tone and symmetric movement during transition.
topics.remember: Transition involves several systems together; weak feeding or poor tone can accompany illness even when one vital sign appears reassuring.

topics.title: Newborn reflexes
topics.recognize: Rooting/sucking support feeding; Moro, grasp, stepping, tonic-neck and Babinski responses help assess neurologic function.
topics.act: Check expected responses and symmetry while considering gestational age and infant state; assess coordinated suck-swallow-breathe before oral feeding.
topics.remember: An absent/asymmetric response may suggest injury or neurologic problems; interpret the whole examination rather than diagnosing from one sleepy response.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents newborn reflexes as clues to neurologic function and safe feeding readiness.

topics.title: APGAR scoring
topics.recognize: Apgar scores appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respirations, each zero to two, at one and five minutes.
topics.act: Assess the newborn's condition immediately and provide needed support without waiting for the score; document and repeat scoring as indicated.
topics.remember: Total seven to ten is reassuring; a low score signals concern. Apgar describes transition and never delays resuscitation.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents one- and five-minute Apgar scoring, while urgent breathing support begins immediately when needed.

topics.title: Hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice
topics.recognize: Jaundice in the first 24 hours needs prompt evaluation; bilirubin risk depends on age in hours, gestation and other factors.
topics.act: Obtain ordered bilirubin assessment, support feeding and prescribed phototherapy; protect eyes and monitor temperature, hydration and output during treatment.
topics.remember: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can injure the brain. Do not label all jaundice after day one harmless or treat by appearance alone.
topics.mnemonic: The clock represents age-in-hours interpretation of jaundice, especially urgent assessment during the first day.

topics.title: Vernix/lanugo/milia/erythema toxicum
topics.recognize: Vernix is a protective white coating; lanugo is fine hair; milia are small white facial bumps; erythema toxicum is a common transient rash.
topics.act: Describe appearance/distribution, provide gentle skin care and assess accompanying symptoms or unusual changes.
topics.remember: Familiar benign findings differ from central cyanosis, infection signs or an ill-appearing newborn; the skin finding must fit the complete assessment.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents identifying normal newborn skin findings by appearance while noticing signs of illness.
topics.sn_note: Original assessment handout retained. Use the course classification: preterm is before 37 weeks; postterm is at least 42 weeks, despite this handout’s older over-40-week label.

topics.title: Fontanelles/sutures/molding/caput/cephalhematoma
topics.recognize: Molding reshapes the skull after birth; caput is scalp edema that crosses sutures, while cephalhematoma is blood beneath periosteum and does not.
topics.act: Assess head shape, sutures/fontanelles and swelling; report concerning progression and monitor jaundice risk with cephalhematoma.
topics.remember: A bulging fontanelle can suggest raised pressure; a sunken one can suggest dehydration. Interpret findings with infant state and clinical status.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents comparing swelling with suture boundaries: caput crosses; cephalhematoma stays within them.
topics.sn_note: Original assessment handout retained. Use the course classification: preterm is before 37 weeks; postterm is at least 42 weeks, despite this handout’s older over-40-week label.

topics.title: Newborn medications (required/recommended)
topics.recognize: Newborn prophylaxis includes vitamin K for bleeding prevention, erythromycin eye ointment for gonococcal infection prevention and indicated hepatitis B immunization.
topics.act: Verify maternal infection status, orders, consent requirements and administration details; explain each purpose and document care.
topics.remember: Vitamin K is not a vaccine. Eye prophylaxis does not replace assessment or treatment of an infant with infection signs.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents three different protections: bleeding prevention, eye prophylaxis and immunization.

topics.title: Metabolic screening
topics.recognize: Metabolic screening identifies selected inherited/metabolic/endocrine conditions before symptoms may appear; an infant can look well and still need testing.
topics.act: Obtain the required specimen at the prescribed age, document feeding/collection circumstances and ensure results, recalls or repeat specimens receive follow-up.
topics.remember: Screening flags risk rather than confirming every diagnosis; early discharge or early collection may require repeat testing under the screening program.
topics.mnemonic: The eye represents screening an apparently well newborn for disorders that are not yet visible.

topics.title: Circumcision
topics.recognize: Circumcision requires informed consent, analgesia and suitability assessment; hypospadias/epispadias may require preserving foreskin for repair.
topics.act: Monitor bleeding, pain and voiding; teach gentle device-specific care and signs needing help.
topics.remember: Gomco/Mogen clamps are removed; a Plastibell ring remains until it separates. Do not pull off the ring or scrub away normal yellow healing film.

topics.title: Initiating and maintaining newborn respirations
topics.recognize: At birth assess breathing, tone and color; apnea, gasping, grunting, retractions or central cyanosis requires immediate attention.
topics.act: Dry/warm, position the airway and promptly support breathing with the neonatal team according to the resuscitation protocol.
topics.remember: Do not wait for the one-minute Apgar to help a newborn who is not breathing; ventilation takes priority over completing routine measurements.
topics.mnemonic: The airway symbol represents breathing support taking priority over routine newborn measurements.

topics.title: Methods of heat loss
topics.recognize: Evaporation loses heat from wet skin; conduction transfers heat to a cold surface; convection involves moving air; radiation involves nearby cold objects.
topics.act: Dry promptly, use warm surfaces, reduce drafts and keep away from cold windows; use skin-to-skin/warming appropriately.
topics.remember: Cold stress increases oxygen and glucose use, raising hypoxia, hypoglycemia and acidosis risk.

topics.title: Altered gestational age or weight
topics.recognize: Prematurity concerns organ maturity; small/large for gestational age concerns weight relative to age. Both affect feeding, temperature and glucose risk.
topics.act: Assess gestational age and growth category, monitor warmth/glucose/respirations and verify feeding coordination; prepare additional support as indicated.
topics.remember: Size does not establish maturity: a large infant may have immature lungs; a small term infant is not automatically premature. Postterm means at least 42 weeks.
topics.mnemonic: The growth symbol represents two separate measurements: gestational maturity and size for that age.
topics.sn_note: Original assessment handout retained. Use the course classification: preterm is before 37 weeks; postterm is at least 42 weeks, despite this handout’s older over-40-week label.

topics.title: Respiratory distress syndrome/surfactant
topics.recognize: Surfactant deficiency makes immature lungs difficult to expand, producing tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions or cyanosis.
topics.act: Obtain neonatal help, support prescribed oxygen/ventilation, temperature and glucose care, and prepare surfactant therapy when ordered.
topics.remember: Antenatal corticosteroids promote lung maturation; surfactant replacement treats deficiency after birth. Birth weight alone does not establish lung maturity.

topics.title: Meconium aspiration syndrome
topics.recognize: Meconium exposure can accompany respiratory distress from aspiration; assess the newborn rather than assuming stained fluid alone proves aspiration syndrome.
topics.act: Alert the neonatal team, assess breathing/heart rate and support ventilation according to the resuscitation plan; monitor oxygenation and ongoing distress.
topics.remember: Meconium-stained fluid is a risk cue. Respiratory assessment determines urgency, and necessary breathing support must not be delayed.
topics.mnemonic: The airway symbol represents assessing and supporting breathing when meconium aspiration is a concern.

topics.title: Apnea / apparent life threatening event (ALE)
topics.recognize: Apnea is a pause of at least 20 seconds, or a shorter pause with concerning bradycardia/color change; preterm infants are vulnerable.
topics.act: Assess breathing, heart rate and oxygenation immediately and provide indicated neonatal support; investigate the cause.
topics.remember: ALTE/ALE is older terminology. BRUE describes a resolved unexplained episode after assessment; a newborn does not meet the lower-risk age criterion.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents a breathing pause with color or heart-rate change requiring immediate assessment.

topics.title: Sudden infant death syndrome
topics.recognize: SIDS is an unexplained infant death after evaluation; sleep-environment risk reduction is central to prevention teaching.
topics.act: Teach supine sleep on a firm, flat separate surface without pillows, loose bedding or soft objects; promote room-sharing without bed-sharing and avoid smoke exposure.
topics.remember: Supervised awake tummy time is different from sleep positioning; prone sleep is not the safe-sleep default.
topics.mnemonic: The shield represents a safe sleep environment: back, firm flat surface and no soft bedding.

topics.title: Newborns at risk for maternal infections
topics.recognize: Maternal infection, prolonged membrane rupture, prematurity or inadequate GBS prophylaxis can increase newborn infection risk. Signs may include temperature instability, poor feeding, apnea or lethargy.
topics.act: Review exposure history, assess subtle changes and promptly escalate for ordered cultures, antibiotics and support.
topics.remember: Newborn sepsis may cause low or unstable temperature rather than obvious fever; apparent sleepiness can be illness.
topics.mnemonic: The alarm represents subtle neonatal infection signs, including temperature instability and poor feeding.

topics.title: Neonatal drug withdrawal / Fetal alcohol syndrome
topics.recognize: Withdrawal may cause tremors, high-pitched cry, irritability, increased tone and feeding problems. Fetal alcohol syndrome involves growth, facial and neurodevelopmental effects.
topics.act: Use structured assessment, reduce overstimulation, support feeding/family care and administer prescribed withdrawal treatment when indicated.
topics.remember: Withdrawal is a post-exposure adaptation; alcohol-related developmental injury is a different process. There is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy.
topics.mnemonic: The brain represents the distinction between newborn withdrawal symptoms and alcohol-related developmental injury.
topics.sn_note: This original covers withdrawal; the companion FTT & FAS handout covers fetal alcohol syndrome.
